posts.title: Parking without the meter
posts.excerpt: Renfrew Council wanted to remove 300 meters. We made sure nobody got a fine because of it.
posts.content:
Client

Renfrew Council

Role

Service designer, then UI for the app and texts

Timeline

January to August 2024

Team

Me, a council product owner, an agency developer

Platform

SMS, iOS and Android, street signs

The council was removing coin meters in Paisley town centre. Two thirds of parking fines were already for people who had paid, but for the wrong zone.

In this case study
  1. The problem
  2. Research
  3. The new flow
  4. Options
  5. Results

Stage 1 of 3

Research

The problem

Two thirds of fines in the town centre went to people who had paid. They had paid for the wrong zone. The zone number was on a sticker on the meter.

The meters were about to be removed, and with them the stickers.

Hypothesis

If people pay by street name instead of zone number, wrong-zone fines will mostly disappear.

Constraints

Existing supplier

The payment back end was a national supplier we could not replace.

Older drivers

A third of permit holders are over 65 and pay by text.

Signs

New street signs had to go through a council committee.

How we researched it

Fine appeals

We read 400 appeal letters from 2023. Half named a street, none named a zone.

Car park interviews

38 drivers in the Lagoon Centre car park and on Causeyside Street.

Text diary

12 permit holders texted us every time they parked for two weeks.

What we learned

  1. Nobody knows their zone. Every appeal letter describes a street.
  2. Texts beat the app. People over 50 preferred a text they could send without unlocking anything.
  3. Reminders matter more than payment. Most fines were for overstaying by under ten minutes.

“I paid. I have the receipt. It just says P4 and I parked on Gauze Street.”

Appeal letter, October 2023

Stage 2 of 3

Design

The new flow

Street

Type or pick the street

Time

Pick how long, price shown

Pay

Card, Apple Pay or text

Reminder

Text ten minutes before it runs out

Wireframes

The same four steps work by text: send the street name and the hours to 60070.

Options we tried

Zone map in the app

Dropped

Tested badly. People could not find themselves on it.

Street name search

Kept

Matches how people describe where they parked.

Pay by text

Kept

Cheapest to run and most used by older drivers.

Before and after

Before

After

What changed: the unit people pay for. It is now a street, which the council maps to a zone behind the scenes.

Stage 3 of 3

Results

Usability testing

Two rounds with 10 drivers each, in their own cars.

Task
Old flow
New flow

Pay for one hour on Gauze Street

6 of 10

10 of 10

Extend by 30 minutes

4 of 10

9 of 10

What happened

Fines for wrong zone, per month

Council enforcement data, first three months

Before

312

After

41

Appeals upheld

Council appeals team

Before

58%

After

12%

Numbers are for the town centre only. The rest of Renfrewshire switches in 2026.

Nadia is the only designer who asked to see our complaint letters. Half the redesign came out of that folder.

Aoife Byrne, parking services manager, Renfrew Council

What I would do differently

I left the street signs until last. They took the longest to approve, and the app was ready months before the signs were up.

Credits

Service design and UI: Nadia Branković. Product owner: Aoife Byrne. Development: Kelvin Digital.

posts.title: Self-checkout for a clothing chain
posts.excerpt: Kilt & Co. customers paid, then waited for staff to remove tags. We moved the tag step first.
posts.content:
Client

Kilt & Co., 14 stores

Role

Product designer, research and UI

Timeline

May to November 2023

Team

Me, a retail operations lead, the till software vendor

Platform

Self-checkout kiosks, 21 inch

Self-checkouts at Kilt & Co. were meant to shorten queues. They made new ones, at the security desk.

In this case study
  1. The problem
  2. Journey map
  3. Before and after
  4. Results

Stage 1 of 3

Research

The problem

Customers paid, then waited for staff to remove security tags. The tag step came after payment, so every customer ended up at the staffed desk anyway.

At weekends the queue for tags was longer than the old till queue.

Hypothesis

If tag removal comes before payment, while the basket is still open, most customers will never need staff.

Constraints

Vendor software

We could change the order of screens but not add new hardware.

Tag types

Three kinds of tag, only one removable by the customer.

How we researched it

Store observation

Four weeks in eight stores, Saturdays included.

Staff diary

Floor staff logged every call to the kiosk for a week.

What we learned

  1. Most items had the easy tag. 80% of items used the magnetic tag that the kiosk pad can release.
  2. Staff calls were about tags. 7 of 10 calls to the kiosk were for tags.

“I have paid. Why am I in another queue?”

Customer, Princes Street store, June 2023

Journey map

Scan

Scan each item

Fine

Pay

Card

Fine

Bag

Bag the items

Alarm goes off at the door

Wait

Queue at the desk for tags

Up to 9 minutes on Saturdays

Rows: what people do, then what goes wrong. The lime cell is where most people gave up.

Stage 2 of 3

Design

The new flow

Scan

Items go on the pad

Tags

Pad releases magnetic tags

Bag

Items into the bag

Pay

Card or phone

Wireframes

We tried three orders on paper at the Princes Street store before touching the software.

Before and after

Before

After

What changed: one step moved from after payment to before it.

Screens

Stage 3 of 3

Results

What happened

Median wait for staff at the kiosk

Store timings, 8 stores

Before

2 min 40 s

After

52 s

Calls to staff per 100 sales

Kiosk logs, 4 weeks

Before

64

After

19

Two stores with the older tag system are excluded.

We moved one screen and the Saturday queue went away. I wish every project was that cheap.

Morag Sinclair, head of stores, Kilt & Co.

What I would do differently

I should have asked the vendor about screen order in week one. We spent two weeks assuming it was fixed.

Credits

Research and design: Nadia Branković. Operations: Morag Sinclair. Software: the till vendor’s Glasgow team.

posts.title: Live departures on the platform
posts.excerpt: Bus stop displays and a phone view that agree with each other, for the first time.
posts.content:
Client

Strathclyde bus partnership

Role

Product designer, displays and app

Timeline

September 2021 to June 2022

Team

Me, two operators, a data engineer

Platform

LED stop displays, phone web view

The stop displays and the app used two different data feeds, so they often disagreed by several minutes. People trusted neither.

In this case study
  1. The problem
  2. Research
  3. The new flow
  4. Results

Stage 1 of 3

Research

The problem

The display and the app disagreed at 4 in 10 stops. Displays used the timetable, the app used live GPS.

People at the stop checked both and believed the worse one.

Hypothesis

If the display and the phone show the same live times in the same words, people will trust them and stop checking both.

Constraints

LED displays

Four lines of amber text, 24 characters each.

Two operators

Two bus companies, two data formats.

How we researched it

Stop interviews

30 people at six stops, evenings and in the rain.

Feed comparison

Two weeks of both feeds side by side for 40 stops.

What we learned

  1. People read the first line only. Almost nobody read past the next bus.
  2. Minutes beat clock times. 2 min was understood faster than 17:42.

“The sign says 4 minutes, the app says 11. I just stand here.”

Passenger at Paisley Road Toll, November 2021

Stage 2 of 3

Design

The new flow

Feed

One merged live feed

Stop display

Next four buses in minutes

Phone

Same list, same words

Fallback

Timetable time marked as scheduled

Before and after

Before

After

What changed: one feed, one wording, minutes instead of clock times.

Screens

Stage 3 of 3

Results

What happened

Stops where display and app disagree

Feed comparison, 40 stops

Before

41%

After

3%

People who said they trust the display

Stop survey, 120 people

Before

28%

After

71%

Survey numbers are from the six stops in the pilot.

We had spent years arguing about whose data was right. Nadia made us agree on one list.

Graham Doyle, network manager, Strathclyde bus partnership

What I would do differently

We designed for sunny screenshots. The first night of rain showed the amber was too dim at two stops.

Credits

Design: Nadia Branković. Data: Fiona Clark. Operators: two Strathclyde bus companies.

posts.title: The order of questions
posts.excerpt: A talk from UX Scotland 2024: reorder a form before you redesign it.
posts.content:
Every service I have worked on had a form that asked the right questions in the wrong order. The ticket machine asked for a fare zone before a destination. The parking app asked for a zone before a street. The pension onboarding asked for a salary before explaining why.

Why order matters more than layout

People answer the question they came with first. If the first screen asks something else, they either guess or leave. On a ticket machine, a third of people left.

Before you touch the visual design, write down the questions in the order a person would say them out loud. Then build the screens in that order.

posts.title: Research on a platform in the rain
posts.excerpt: Notes on doing four-minute interviews next to a ticket machine, and why a hi-vis vest helps.
posts.content:
Most of my research happens on platforms and pavements. People are in a hurry, it is often raining, and nobody wants to sign a consent form.

What works

  • Wear a hi-vis vest and stand next to station staff. People assume you are official and helpful, which you are.
  • Ask one question: what were you trying to do just now? Then listen for four minutes.
  • Write the answer on a card straight away, with the time and the station.
  • Offer a coffee voucher after, not before.

You will get fewer words than in a lab. You will get the real problem much faster.
